query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior in HfNbTaTiZr arises from a coupling between temperature‐dependent local lattice distortions and residual thermal stresses generated by thermal expansion mismatch. At high temperature, thermal expansion relaxes local distortions leading to lower apparent creep resistance, while at lower temperatures and after cold working, the enhanced local strain fields (and any potential short-range atomic ordering from aging at 600–800 °C) increase dislocation pinning and microhardness. This unified mechanism explains the disparate observations in tensile creep, cold-rolled hardness, and elastic moduli trends.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized, conventionally processed HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with a high degree of configurational disorder and inherent local lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Prepare samples with two distinct thermal histories: one maintained in the as-cast state (with full residual thermal stresses) and one annealed to partially relieve residual stresses. Subject both sets to controlled cold rolling, tensile creep tests at ~1250 °C, and elastic modulus measurements from 293 to 1100 K. Apply intermediate aging treatments at 600–800 °C to probe potential short-range ordering effects.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing performed over a broad temperature range (room temperature up to 1250 °C), with cold rolling applied under identical deformation conditions and aging treatments held constant at 600–800 °C for a defined duration. Thermal treatments must be executed to isolate the effect of residual stresses from intrinsic lattice distortions.
generation.structural_mediator: Temperature-dependent local lattice distortions that are amplified or relaxed by thermal expansion mismatch-induced residual stresses, and possibly modified by short-range ordering during aging.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures and after cold working, local lattice distortions and residual stresses increase dislocation pinning, leading to higher microhardness and elastic modulus. At high temperatures (e.g., during creep at 1250 °C), thermal expansion promotes lattice relaxation reducing these distortions, thus lowering resistance to dislocation motion (faster creep). Aging at 600–800 °C may induce short-range ordering that further pins dislocations, thereby increasing strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with samples whose residual stresses have been partially relieved via annealing, as-cast samples should exhibit higher microhardness after cold rolling, a steeper increase in elastic modulus at lower temperatures, and lower creep rates at 1250 °C. Additionally, aging should accentuate these effects by promoting additional dislocation pinning via short-range ordering.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy state with its inherent residual stresses and lattice distortion, without any additional stress-relieving annealing.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected to be operative across the temperature domains previously studied: room temperature for cold-rolled microhardness, 293–1100 K for elastic moduli, 600–800 °C during aging treatments, and around 1250 °C during tensile creep. It is also most relevant in processing scenarios where thermal expansion mismatch (e.g., during composite solidification) induces significant residual stresses.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how quantitatively dominant the short-range ordering effects (from aging) are relative to the inherent residual stresses and local lattice distortion. The precise balance between thermal relaxation and distortion retention across the temperature range also requires further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one in the as-cast state and one subjected to a stress-relieving anneal. Apply identical cold rolling, aging (at 600–800 °C), tensile creep (at ~1250 °C), and elastic modulus (293–1100 K) tests to both sets. Use TEM and XRD to assess differences in local lattice distortion and any short-range ordering. Compare the mechanical properties of the two sets.
measurements: Elastic modulus versus temperature from 293 to 1100 K
TEM/XRD characterization of lattice distortion and ordering
Thermal expansion measurements to infer residual stresses
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed samples (with reduced residual stresses) do not show a significant reduction in microhardness, do not exhibit a modified elastic modulus trend (i.e., a less pronounced temperature dependence), or if creep rates at high temperature are indistinguishable from the as-cast samples (within experimental uncertainty), then the hypothesis that thermal expansion mismatch and local lattice distortions govern the observed behavior is falsified.
